title: AVATAR_MVT_David Chou
description: David Chou, M.D., Ph.D., Principal Scientist Emulate; the Mission Verification Test (MVT) for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) payload, marking a critical milestone ahead of the Artemis II launch. This test validated system performance as designed to confirm mission readiness. ; The AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation will use organ-on-a-chip devices, or organ chips, to study the effects of increased radiation and microgravity on human health.
via: the NASA Image and Video Library

transcript.text: - My name's David Chow.
My last name is spelled CHOU.
I'm the principal investigator of Avatar at Emulate.
So Avatar is a pathfinding mission.
It is an experiment where we are going
to create individualized bone marrow chips from astronauts
flying on Artemis two.
And we are going to observe how those bone marrow chips
respond to the stressors of space flight
because they're flying
around the moon along with the astronauts.
And we are hoping to see whether
or not those chips model individualized
responses to space flight.
Yeah, so today is what we call the day of chip seeding.
And so this is the day
where we actually take the previously frozen astronaut
blood progenitor cells that we've out of the freezer
and we thaw them and we put them into the bone marrow
chips themselves.
They'll be seated in a chip that has two channels,
the top and the bottom channel.
And the top channel is
where the astronaut cells are gonna go, along
with bone marrow supporting stromal cells.
And these chips are then going to be perfused
with medium through the bottom and kept overnight.
And then the following day, we are gonna give the chips over
to Space Tango, who will then hook up the chips
to their custom hardware that's gonna profuse these chips
for the duration of Artemis two, with the capability
of using these organ chips as avatars of human organs,
that means we could potentially send up many more
human organ chips than we could possibly send astronauts.
In addition, we can send human organ chips
that model a variety of tissues that would be difficult
to sample in a human, for example, the brain or the heart.
We could send up many more chips
and we can get
deep biological information from many different organs
that we couldn't otherwise get.
There are two well-established stressors that occur
as a result of space flight.
The first is the increased amount of radiation
that the astronauts experience,
and then the second is the lack of gravity
or rather microgravity.
So those are the two primary stressors for us,
especially with the bone marrow.
The bone marrow is possibly the most radio
sensitive organ in the body.
And so we're expecting that a lot
of the biologic changes we observe to be driven primarily
by the increased radiation.
So if the project works out
as we are hoping it will, then that means that
these organ chips can respond
to space flight stressors in an individualized manner.
And that has potential implications for how we do,
for example, clinical trials in the future.
It has implications for how we test drugs both for efficacy
and toxicity in the future.
And I think those are the, that's the primary
potential application for how this project could affect
medicine here on earth.
So when we were developing the bone marrow chip,
we tested our model system against standard
suspension cultures, which are
what are widely used in the field.
And what we found is that if you study
how the bone marrow chips respond to drugs, we can model
human drug exposures in a way
that you couldn't do in standard suspension culture.
And we see much
and we are able to more accurately predict how those,
how the human bone marrow responds to drugs
as a result of that.
The thing is, standard suspension cultures are really only
single cell types in a 96 well plate
or some other type of Petri dish correction
or some other type of standard plastic standard
lab plastic wear.
But with the bone marrow chip, we have the fact
that these chips are cultured in three dimensions.
The cells are cultured in three dimensions.
And furthermore, we have multiple cell types,
not only the bone marrow progenitor cells,
but also the supporting stromal cells which
talk to the bone marrow progenitor.
So when we were creating the bone marrow chip,
we compared it side by side
with standard suspension cultures in lab,
standard lab plastic wear.
And what we found is that the ability
to put the chips in three dimensional culture
and to culture, not the progenitor cells, only on their own,
but in combination with the supporting stromal cells,
we find that the behavior of the cells is different in
how they differentiate and how they respond to drugs.
And so really it seems to be,
at least in our hands when we've tested it,
a better predictor of how
the bone marrow in your body responds to a variety
of stressors as opposed to standard cultures.
So there are a variety of cellular changes
that have been described in previous studies
via other labs.
So Chris Mason's lab, pat Jameson's lab at UCSD
and other labs have already studied what happens
to cells at least in low earth orbit.
And we expect that some of those changes,
including DNA damage, increased reactive oxygen species,
mitochondrial dysfunction, increased secretion
of different inflammatory factors will likely
be observed in this experiment as well.
It's the first time that we're looking at this
outside of low earth orbit.
And so that may change to some degree the degree
to which those changes happen, but we don't know that yet.
And we're also studying types of cells
that haven't been well studied in the past
because we're looking at the process of hematopoiesis.
And so almost all the studies previously have looked at
mature cells circulating in the blood.
We are actually modeling the process
of blood cell development in the bone marrow.
And so we are actually gonna be observing the effects
of space flight on some of those earlier stages
of blood cell development.
And so we don't really know what we're going
to see, but we're excited.
So we're going to be running a variety
of assays concurrently.
So the most important readout that we're going
to be doing is we're gonna be taking the cells out
of the chip and we're gonna be doing something called single
cell RNA sequencing.
So this is an assay where we can look at thousands of cells
across all the different bone marrow chips, as well
as crew member blood samples.
And we're gonna look within each cell to see
what genes are being expressed
and to what degree they're being expressed.
And the other assays that we're going
to do include staining the cells for a variety
of DNA damage markers.
We're also gonna be looking in the plasma of the astronauts
and potentially the outflows of the bone marrow chips
to see if there are inflammatory cytokines
that have been secreted.
Okay. What's the long-term vision
for this technology in space health research?
So I think NASA probably has a variety of plans
for the organ ships.
From my view, my understanding is that
they are very interested in testing whether
or not these chips can respond in an individualized
fashion to space flight.
And so this means, for example,
that you could send chips from people who are much older
or much younger than the typical astronaut.
You could send chips from people with a variety
of medical comorbidities.
And so you can get a much better understanding of
how the general population will respond
to space flight in a way that you couldn't do otherwise.
